items.title: Three Dilemmas That Dismantle "Manifestation Without Production"

items.zh: 應審問彼：汝何所欲？為無障緣而有障礙？為有障緣耶？若無障緣者，無障礙緣而有障礙，不應道理。若有障緣者，屬果之因何故不障？同是有故，不應道理。譬如黑闇障瓫中水，亦能障瓫。若言障緣亦障因者，亦應顯因，俱被障故。而言但顯因中先有果性，不顯因者，不應道理。
items.en: One should press them thus: what, precisely, do you mean — is there no obstructing condition at all, yet an obstruction is present? Or is there an obstructing condition? If there is no obstructing condition, then to say an obstruction is present with no obstructing condition present makes no sense. If there is an obstructing condition, then why does it not equally obstruct the cause to which the effect belongs, since both equally exist? This makes no sense — just as darkness obstructing the water within a jar equally obstructs the jar itself. And if you say the obstructing condition obstructs the cause as well, then the cause too should be manifested once it is removed, since both were equally obstructed — yet to say only the effect already present within the cause is manifested, and not the cause, makes no sense either.

items.zh: 復應問彼：為有性是障緣？為果性耶？若有性是障緣者，是即有性常不顯了，不應道理。因亦是有，何不為障？若言果性是障緣者，是則一法亦因亦果，如芽是種子果，是莖等因，是即一法亦顯不顯，不應道理。
items.en: One should further press them: is it the effect's latent existence within the cause that the obstructing condition obstructs, or specifically its nature as an effect? If it is that latent existence that is obstructed, then existence itself should perpetually remain unmanifested — which makes no sense, since the cause too exists, and yet is never said to be obstructed. If it is the nature of being an effect that is obstructed, then consider that one and the same phenomenon is often both an effect and a cause at once — a sprout is the effect of its seed, yet the cause of the stalk that follows it — so that one and the same thing would have to be simultaneously manifested and unmanifested, which makes no sense.

items.zh: 又今問汝，隨汝意答。本法與顯為異不異？若不異者，法應常顯，顯已復顯，不應道理。若言異者，彼顯為無因耶？為有因耶？若言無因，無因而顯，不應道理。若有因者，果性可顯，非是因性，以不顯因能顯於果，不應道理。如是無障緣故，有障緣故，有相故，果相故，顯不異故，顯異故，不應道理。
items.en: Further, I now ask you, answer as you see fit: is the original phenomenon identical to, or different from, its manifestation? If not different, then the phenomenon should always already be manifest — to then speak of it being "manifested" again makes no sense. If different, then is that manifestation itself uncaused, or caused? If uncaused, then an uncaused manifestation makes no sense. If caused, then it is only the effect's own nature that becomes manifest, never the cause's — and manifesting an effect without ever manifesting its cause makes no sense either.

items.title: Why "Unseen" Never Means "Nonexistent," and the Sound-Theorists Fall the Same Way

items.zh: 是故汝言：若法性無，是即無相，若法性有，是即有相。性若是無，不可顯了，性若是有，方可顯了者；不應道理。我今當說：雖復是有，不可取相。謂或有遠故，雖有而不可取。又由四種障因障故，而不可取。復由極微細故，而不可取。或由心散亂故，而不可取。或由根損壞故，而不可取。或由未得彼相應智故，而不可取。
items.en: Therefore, your claim — that if a phenomenon's nature is absent, it has no characteristic, and if its nature is present, it has a characteristic; that if its nature is absent, it cannot be manifested, and if its nature is present, only then can it be manifested — does not accord with reason. I shall now state the matter correctly: a thing may indeed exist, and yet its characteristic still not be apprehensible. This may be because it is too distant, and so, though existing, is not apprehensible. It may be because it is obstructed by one of four kinds of obstruction. It may be because it is exceedingly subtle. It may be because the mind is distracted. It may be because a faculty is impaired. Or it may be because one has not yet attained the wisdom that corresponds to it.

items.title: The Sound-Theorists Fall the Same Way, and the Second Doctrine Closes

items.zh: 如因果顯了論不應道理，當知聲相論者亦不應理。此中差別者，外聲論師起如是見，立如是論：聲相常住，無生無滅；然由宣吐方得顯了。是故此論如顯了論，非應理說。
items.en: Just as the doctrine of manifestation through condition does not accord with reason, so too the Sound-nature theorists' doctrine should be understood as unreasonable. Their distinctive claim is this: non-Buddhist Sound-theorists hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that the nature of sound is permanent, neither arising nor ceasing, and is merely made manifest through its utterance. This doctrine, therefore, like the doctrine of manifestation, is not a soundly reasoned teaching.

items.title: The Third Doctrine: Do Past and Future Truly, Substantially Exist?

items.zh: 去來實有論者，謂如有一，若沙門、若婆羅門、若在此法者，由不正思惟故，起如是見，立如是論：有過去，有未來，其相成就，猶如現在，實有非假。
items.en: The doctrine that past and future truly exist: there are certain renunciants, brahmins, or even those within this very teaching who, through unsound reflection, hold such a view and establish such a doctrine — that the past exists, the future exists, their characteristics fully accomplished exactly as the present's are, truly existing rather than merely nominal.

items.zh: 問：何因緣故，彼起如是見，立如是論？答：由教及理故。教如前說。又在此法者，於如來經不如理分別故。
謂如經言：一切有者，即十二處。此十二處，實相是有。又薄伽梵說有過去業。又說有過去色、有未來色，廣說乃至識亦如是。
items.en: That is: as the sūtra states, "all that exists" refers to the twelve sense-bases — and so, they reason, these twelve sense-bases truly, substantially exist. Further, the Blessed One spoke of past karma existing. Further, he spoke of past form existing and future form existing, and so on in full detail through consciousness as well.

items.zh: 理者，謂如有一，為性尋思，為性觀察，廣說如前。

items.title: Why They Thought Denying Past and Future Would Destroy Karma and Cognition

items.zh: 彼如是思：若法自相安住，此法真實是有。此若未來無者，爾時應未受相；此若過去無者，爾時應失自相。若如是者，諸法自相應不成就。由此道理，亦非真實，故不應理。由是思惟，起如是見，立如是論：過去、未來性相實有。
items.en: They reason thus: if a phenomenon's own characteristic remains established, that phenomenon truly exists. Were this phenomenon nonexistent while future, it would, at that time, never have taken on its characteristic at all; were it nonexistent once past, it would, at that time, have already lost its own characteristic. Were this so, no phenomenon's own characteristic could ever be genuinely established — and by this reasoning, nothing would be truly real, which makes no sense. Reasoning in this way, they arrive at this view, and establish this doctrine: that the characteristics of the past and future truly, substantially exist.

items.title: Two Dilemmas: Is a Past or Future Thing the Same as, or Different From, a Present One?

items.zh: 應審問彼：汝何所欲？去來二相與現在相為一為異？若言相一，立三世相，不應道理。若相異者，性相實有，不應道理。
items.en: One should press them thus: what, precisely, do you mean — are the characteristics of the past and future the same as, or different from, the characteristic of the present? If you say they are the same, then establishing three distinct times makes no sense. If they are different, then claiming past and future substantially, truly exist just as the present does makes no sense.

items.zh: 又汝應說自意所欲？墮三世法、為是常相？為無常相？若常相者，墮在三世，不應道理。若無常相，於三世中恒是實有，不應道理。
items.en: Further, you should state what you actually intend: is a phenomenon falling within the three times permanent in character, or impermanent? If permanent, then for it to fall within three distinct times at all makes no sense. If impermanent, then for it to be equally, perpetually, truly existent throughout all three times makes no sense.

blocks.text: Today finishes the second doctrine and opens the third, which concerns Buddhists directly: the Sarvāstivāda view that past and future things truly exist. The argument is careful. Notice how the treatise grants what is true in an opponent's position before showing where it fails.

Untranslated: the formal questions at 0304b27–b29 and 0304c03–c04 ("Why do they hold this view? Through scripture and reasoning … and, within this teaching, through misreading the Tathāgata's sūtras").

If conditions only reveal what already exists, what hides it beforehand? If darkness hides the water in a jar, it hides the jar too; so if something obscures the effect, it should equally obscure the cause, and removing it should reveal both. The treatise presses the point with three dilemmas. Both teachers explain one technical pair: 有性, the mere possibility of an effect with no mark yet perceptible, and 果性, the effect's mark already manifest. Neither can coherently be the "hidden" thing.

The opponent might reply: the effect exists but is not perceived. The treatise agrees that existing things can go unperceived, and lists why: being too far away; the four obstructions of Day 17 (Master Cháng Bǎi and Venerable Miào Jìng both use the stars outshone by the sun); being too subtle; a distracted mind; an impaired faculty; or lacking the corresponding wisdom. Venerable Miào Jìng's example of the last: non-discriminating wisdom can perceive ultimate truth; the truth is there, we have not attained the wisdom.
But none of these applies to the effect in the cause, so the reply fails. The list itself is useful: it is a Yogācāra account of why we fail to perceive what is real.

The **Sound-theorists** (聲論者), associated with the Mīmāṃsā, hold that the sounds of language, above all the Vedas, are eternal and merely manifested by utterance. Venerable Miào Jìng's image of their view: "the bell's sound is eternal, but you must strike it for the sound to come out." The same refutation applies.

The third doctrine: past and future things exist as really as present ones. It is held by some outsiders "and even by those within this very teaching", which both teachers identify as the **Sarvāstivāda** ("the doctrine that all exists"), for whom "the three times truly exist; the substance of dharmas endures".

Their reasons are scriptural and practical. The Buddha said "all that exists" is the twelve sense-bases; he spoke of past karma existing; he spoke of past and future form. Master Cháng Bǎi states their worry: "If the past no longer exists, how can there be present results? If the future doesn't exist, how does rebirth continue?" They fear that without real past and future, karma and memory collapse.

The first refutation: are the marks of past and future the same as the present's, or different? If the same, why speak of three times? If different, past and future are not "truly existent" in the present's sense. Venerable Miào Jìng: Nāgārjuna's *Middle Treatise* refutes the three times with the same "same or different" method. Madhyamaka and Yogācāra agree here: as the *Pīxún jì* says, this is "the general attachment of outsiders and the two vehicles". Tomorrow the treatise answers the opponent's worry about karma.

quiz.q: What image does the text use to ask why an obstructing condition would not also obstruct the cause?
options: darkness hiding the water in a jar hides the jar too
quiz.why: "Just as darkness obstructing the water within a jar equally obstructs the jar itself." Effect and cause both exist; whatever hides one should hide the other, and when removed, reveal both. Master Cháng Bǎi: "If darkness hides the table, why doesn't it hide the room?"

quiz.q: The text lists reasons an existing thing may not be apprehended. Which is NOT among them?
options: because it doesn't exist at all
quiz.why: The whole point is that "a thing may indeed exist, and yet its characteristic still not be apprehensible": distance, four obstructions, subtlety, distraction, impaired faculty, and lacking the corresponding wisdom. A is the very fallacy refuted — "unseen, so nonexistent."

quiz.q: Among the four obstructions, what example do the teachers give for "being outshone" (映障)?
options: once the sun is out, the stars' light is overpowered and they can't be seen by day
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "The stars exist, but once the sun comes out, you can't see them." Venerable Miào Jìng: "Like the sun's brightness overpowering the moon and stars — by day you can't see starlight." C is the obstruction of illusion; D, that of concealment.

quiz.q: The Sound-theorists say sound is permanent and only manifested by utterance. What image does Venerable Miào Jìng use for their view?
options: the bell's sound is permanent, appearing only when struck
quiz.why: Venerable Miào Jìng: "The bell's sound is eternal and abiding, but you must strike it for the sound to come out." Master Cháng Bǎi's refutation: without conditions there is no speech; "holding that a sentence exists before it is spoken is wrong" — Buddhism teaches arising from conditions, not revealing by them.

quiz.q: According to the teachers, which Buddhist school is meant by "those within this teaching" who hold the three times to be real?
options: the Sarvāstivāda — "the three times truly exist; the substance of dharmas endures"
quiz.why: Master Cháng Bǎi: "Within Buddhism there is the Sarvāstivāda, who also hold the three times real and the substance of dharmas abiding." Venerable Miào Jìng: "These objections are aimed at the Sarvāstivāda … a Hīnayāna school." A is the self-doctrine's school.

quiz.q: According to the treatise, on which three scriptural statements does this doctrine rely?
options: "all that exists" is the twelve sense-bases; the Buddha spoke of past karma; and of past and future form through consciousness
quiz.why: "As the sūtra states, 'all that exists' refers to the twelve sense-bases … Further, the Blessed One spoke of past karma existing. Further, he spoke of past form existing and future form existing, and so on … through consciousness." §14–16 give the hidden intent of each. Master Cháng Bǎi: their reasoning is, "Why else would the Buddha say 'exists' rather than 'nominally exists'?"

quiz.q: The text asks whether the marks of past and future are the same as or different from the present's. What fault does each answer bring?
options: if the same, positing three times makes no sense; if different, claiming past and future truly exist makes no sense
quiz.why: "If you say they are the same, then establishing three distinct times makes no sense. If they are different, then claiming past and future substantially, truly exist … makes no sense." Master Cháng Bǎi: "Since the present is real, whatever differs from it — past and future — should be nonexistent"; the *Pixunji*: only present dharmas, arisen and not ceased, have perceptible marks.
